code_findings.title: When the initial httpx probe to localhost:9223 returns HTTP 200, the new test takes the reuse path and never invokes its subprocess mock, so its remote-debugging launch-argument assertion is not execu
code_findings.explanation: The complete test body patches requests.get but does not patch httpx. The production method performs its initial probe with httpx; on status 200 it connects through the mocked DummyChromium and returns immediately. The test's only assertion about the subprocess arguments is inside dummy_create_subprocess_exec, which is invoked only on the later launch path. Thus a real service answering 200 on port 9223 bypasses that assertion while still producing the expected DummyBrowser for the test's result assertion.
code_findings.impact: Caused by the change: The added test mocks requests.get, but the changed custom-port probe is issued through httpx.AsyncClient. Therefore the mock does not control the initial probe. If that probe receives 200, line 213 returns before the launch code at line 229 can call the test's dummy_create_subprocess_exec, leaving the launch-argument assertion at test line 190 unexecuted.

pr_semantic_analysis.change_summary: Browser startup now supports a configurable Chrome remote-debugging port, defaulting to the existing Chrome debug-port constant. The selected port is used when probing for an existing browser, connecting over CDP, constructing launch arguments, and checking port occupancy. User-provided Chrome binaries are now launched through direct argv-based subprocess execution. The agent and file-upload edits appear non-semantic, while the new test targets custom-port startup.

behavior_changes.description: Browser callers can select a Chrome remote-debugging port. For a user-provided browser binary, the browser setup probes and connects to that selected localhost port and supplies the same port when launching Chrome; built-in browser launch also constructs its debugging argument from the selected value rather than a fixed port.
evidence: The configuration model exposes chrome_remote_debugging_port with the prior debug-port constant as its default.
The user-provided-browser path interpolates the configured value into its version endpoint, CDP endpoint, and Chrome launch argument.
The built-in-browser path constructs and conditionally removes the debugging argument for the configured port.

behavior_changes.description: When starting a user-supplied Chrome executable, browser setup now invokes the configured binary directly and passes Chrome options as separate process arguments, rather than routing the launch through the previous subprocess-shell call shape.
evidence: The configured browser executable is passed as the executable argument and the assembled Chrome options are expanded as separate argv entries.

important_symbols.reason: Defines the new externally supplied port setting, its nullable type, and its default, so it controls compatibility and validation behavior for every setup path that consumes the configuration.
Contains the main semantic change: existing-instance discovery, Chrome process launch, readiness polling, and CDP connection are all tied to the configured port.
Moves built-in browser debugging-argument construction and occupied-port handling from the fixed port to the configured port.
Centralizes formatting of the Chrome remote-debugging argument after that argument was removed from the otherwise static CHROME_ARGS collection.
Documents the intended custom-port contract for the launch argument and CDP endpoint, although structural analysis should verify how completely it exercises readiness probing.

investigation_hints.description: Trace all BrowserConfig construction, serialization, aliases, and wrappers to determine where custom or null debugging-port values can enter and whether validation is imposed elsewhere.
Follow browser selection and lifecycle control to establish when the user-provided path versus built-in path runs, and how process ownership and cleanup behave when an existing browser is reused.
Inspect Chrome and Playwright assumptions around debugging-port arguments, duplicate flags, occupied ports, readiness polling, and CDP connection behavior.

local_risks.description: The configuration explicitly accepts null for the debugging port, but setup interpolates that value into a localhost URL and passes it to the socket port check. A caller supplying null can therefore reach malformed endpoint construction or an invalid socket-port operation instead of receiving an early configuration-validation error.

The generated debugging-port flag and caller-provided extra arguments are deduplicated through an unordered set. If extra_browser_args contains a different remote-debugging-port flag, both values can survive with non-guaranteed ordering; depending on Chrome's duplicate-flag precedence, Chrome could listen on a different port from the one subsequently used for readiness and CDP connection.
